lead: Thermodynamics becomes calculable when a system has one pressure and one temperature. Equilibrium gives that condition: no temperature difference, no unbalanced force, no reaction still driving change. A quasi-static process keeps equilibrium while the state changes by moving in tiny steps. The process then forms a continuous line on a p–V diagram, so its area can be used. Turbine analysis, gas compression and steam plant design rest on this idealisation.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for state, path and process, and 1.2 for what may cross a boundary.

blocks.text: A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when nothing inside it, and nothing across its boundary, is driving a change. Three balances must hold together.

Thermal equilibrium means no temperature difference. Every part and every body it can exchange heat with has the same temperature. Otherwise heat flows and the state drifts. The zeroth law turns this into the definition of temperature.

Mechanical equilibrium means no unbalanced force: pressure is the same at every point and the piston is not accelerating. For gas under a resting piston, p_gas × A = W_piston + p_atm × A with p in Pa, W_piston in N and A in m²; in kPa, p_gas = W_piston/(1000A) + p_atm, where p_gas is gas pressure in kPa, W_piston is piston weight in N, A is piston area in m² and p_atm is outside atmospheric pressure in kPa. Only if the outside of the piston is in vacuum does p_gas = W_piston/(1000A).
Chemical equilibrium means no reaction, mixing or diffusion is still changing composition.

With all three satisfied and the boundary fixed, p, V, T and composition stay constant. Constant readings are the practical test. Read, wait, read again; unchanged readings mean no change. They do not prove equilibrium, as the next section shows.

A steady state means properties at a fixed point do not change with time. It does not mean equilibrium. A running steam turbine shows the difference. Steam enters at 500 °C and leaves at 60 °C. The metal near inlet and outlet hold fixed temperatures, so readings are constant for hours. Yet a temperature gradient sits inside and heat keeps flowing down it.
Equilibrium has no gradients, no throughput, no driving force left. Steady state has gradients fixed in space, continuous flow and a driving force balanced by throughput.
A phone charger left plugged in warms for ten minutes, then stops changing. It is steady, not equilibrium: electrical work enters and heat leaves.
Exam question in disguise: constant properties do not prove equilibrium. Ask whether mass or energy is crossing the boundary.

Real changes are usually fast. Open a valve and gas rushes from high to low pressure. For a few seconds p and T differ from point to point. Such non-equilibrium conditions are not equilibrium states, so they have no single p or V and cannot be plotted as points on a p–V diagram.

A quasi-static process (some syllabi say quasi-equilibrium) is slow enough that at every instant the system sits infinitesimally away from equilibrium. It passes through a succession of well-defined equilibrium states. Each state has one p, one V and one T — a point on the p–V diagram.

items: Create a driving force that is infinitesimal: add one grain of sand to the piston (a small compression), or lower the outside pressure by a tiny amount dp (a small change in pressure in kPa; a small expansion).
Wait while the system settles into the new equilibrium state.
Repeat until the final state is reached.
In the limit of infinitely many infinitely small steps, the process is quasi-static.

blocks.text: A quasi-static process can follow any path. The worked example uses one particular path: if the product pV stays constant, then pV = C, where p is absolute pressure in kPa, V is volume in m³ and C is a constant in kPa·m³ = kJ. On a p–V diagram this path is a hyperbola.

blocks.where: p is absolute pressure in kPa, V is volume in m³, and C is a constant in kPa·m³ = kJ. This is the particular path used in the worked example, not a rule for every quasi-static process.

blocks.text: The whole process is then a continuous line from state A to state B. Without a line there is no area, and without area displacement work W = ∫p dV cannot be computed (see 1.7). Infinite steps take infinite time, so no real process is exactly quasi-static; a slow real process is only a good approximation to it.

Quasi-static is about speed, not direction. A gas can be stirred by a paddle wheel while a piston moves in slowly. Pressure stays uniform and the path is a clean line, yet the process is irreversible: paddle work has become internal energy and will not come back on its own.
Friction gives the same result. Push a piston slowly against friction and the state still passes through equilibrium states, but energy leaks to friction and cannot be recovered.
Every reversible process is quasi-static. Not every quasi-static process is reversible. Reversibility needs zero friction, zero viscosity and zero electrical resistance; Unit 3 defines it properly.

figure.caption: Solid chain: quasi-static route with many tiny steps, each landing on a near-equilibrium state, so the path A to B is continuous. Dashed branch: a fast change, which has no single pressure or temperature and cannot be drawn as a line.

spec.title: Quasi-static path
spec.aria: A block diagram shows a slow small step passing through near-equilibrium states from state A to state B, while a fast change branches off to no continuous path.

examples.question: A gas goes from state 1 (p₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 0.20 m³) to state 2 (p₂ = 200 kPa, V₂ = 0.10 m³) along a quasi-static path on which the product pV stays constant. (a) Check whether p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. (b) Find the pressure at V = 0.15 m³. (c) Can this path be drawn as a continuous line on a p–V diagram?
steps: State 1: p₁V₁ = 100 kPa × 0.20 m³ = 20 kPa·m³ = 20 kJ.
The products are equal, so C = 20 kJ and p = C/V.
Every intermediate volume gives one finite pressure, so each state is one equilibrium point. Joining them gives an unbroken hyperbola from (0.20 m³, 100 kPa) to (0.10 m³, 200 kPa).
Volume falls while pressure rises, so the gas is compressed. Answer to (c): yes.
examples.answer: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ = 20 kJ, C = 20 kJ, p = 133.33 kPa at V = 0.15 m³, and the path is a continuous hyperbola on the p–V diagram.
examples.check:
p1, V1 = 100.0, 0.20
p2, V2 = 200.0, 0.10
print(round(p1 * V1, 6))
print(round(p2 * V2, 6))
C = p1 * V1
print(round(C, 6))
print(round(C / 0.15, 2))

traps: Treating quasi-static as reversible. A slow process with friction or paddle-wheel stirring is quasi-static and still irreversible.
Treating constant readings as equilibrium. A turbine or heat exchanger holds steady readings while mass flows and internal gradients stay fixed. That is steady state.

Plotting a fast process as a line. A fast process passes through non-equilibrium conditions, where p and T differ from point to point. These are not equilibrium states, so they have no single p or V and cannot be plotted as points on a p–V diagram; ∫p dV is meaningless for it.
Checking only one balance. Gas at uniform pressure but with a hot end and cold end is not in thermodynamic equilibrium.
Unit slip: kPa × m³ = kJ. So 100 kPa × 0.20 m³ = 20 kJ = 20 000 J, not 20 J.

quiz.q: Define thermodynamic equilibrium in one sentence.
quiz.a: A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium all hold together, so no property changes with time at a fixed boundary.

quiz.q: Name the three conditions that must hold for thermodynamic equilibrium.
quiz.a: Thermal: no temperature difference. Mechanical: no unbalanced force. Chemical: no reaction or diffusion driving a change in composition.

quiz.q: Why can a quasi-static process be drawn as a continuous line on a p–V diagram, while a fast expansion cannot?
quiz.a: In a quasi-static process each intermediate state is an equilibrium state with a single p and a single V, so it is a point, and joined points make a line. In a fast expansion p differs from place to place, so no single p exists and no point can be plotted.

quiz.q: A steam turbine runs for hours with inlet temperature 500 °C and outlet temperature 60 °C, both constant. Is it in thermodynamic equilibrium? Justify.
quiz.a: No. Readings at each point are constant with time, so it is in steady state. But a 440 °C difference exists inside, so thermal equilibrium fails, and mass flows through continuously. Equilibrium needs no gradients and no throughput.

quiz.q: A gas goes from p₁ = 150 kPa, V₁ = 0.30 m³ to p₂ = 300 kPa along a quasi-static path with pV = constant. Find V₂ and the pressure at V = 0.20 m³.
A piston is pushed in slowly while a paddle wheel stirs the gas, and pressure stays uniform throughout. Is the process quasi-static? Is it reversible?
quiz.a: Quasi-static, yes: every intermediate state is an equilibrium state with one p and one T, so the path is a continuous line. Reversible, no: the paddle work has become internal energy through viscous dissipation and cannot be returned.

quiz.q: Separate equilibrium from steady state in one line each, with an example.
quiz.a: Equilibrium: no gradients, no flow, nothing driving — gas in a closed cylinder left alone. Steady state: gradients fixed in space, flow continuous — a running steam turbine with constant inlet and outlet temperatures.

beyond: Not for the exam. Simulators use steady-state blocks with equilibrium flashes inside. Compressors and turbines are first sized as quasi-static, then corrected by efficiency. Finite-time thermodynamics studies machines running at finite rate. Search: endoreversible thermodynamics, quasi-static approximation in turbomachinery, equilibrium flash calculation.
